subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Sencha and Gyokuro
description: A micro-lesson that makes Sencha and Gyokuro usable.

hook.text: Sencha is Japan's everyday tea—bright, grassy, and refreshing. Gyokuro is its luxurious, shaded sibling.

buildup.text: Sencha grows in full sunlight and is steamed immediately after harvest to preserve green freshness.

discovery.text: Gyokuro is shaded for 20 days before picking. Shade boosts amino acids, giving an intense, savory sweetness.

twist.text: That savory richness is called 'umami.' Gyokuro is one of the few teas where umami dominates the flavor.

climax.text: Gyokuro is brewed at just 50–60°C with very little water—almost a tea concentrate, sipped in tiny cups.

punchline.text: Sun gives brightness. Shade gives depth. Both are green tea.

quiz.question: What gives Gyokuro its intense umami flavor?
options: Shading the plants for 20 days boosts amino acids

details.summary: Sencha is Japan's most popular tea, accounting for about 60 percent of production, with a bright, grassy flavor. Gyokuro is its luxury shade-grown cousin, covered for 20 days before harvest to boost umami and sweetness. The shade-growing process transforms the tea's chemistry and price.
details.whyItMatters: Sencha and gyokuro illustrate how a single growing technique, shading, can dramatically change tea flavor and value. Gyokuro is among the most expensive teas in the world.
takeaways: Sencha makes up about 60 percent of Japanese tea production
Gyokuro is shade-grown for 20 days before harvest
Shading increases L-theanine and reduces bitterness

faq.question: What does shade-growing do to tea leaves?
faq.answer: Blocking sunlight prevents the conversion of L-theanine to catechins. This increases sweetness and umami while reducing astringency. Leaves also produce more chlorophyll, turning deeper green. The concentrated amino acids give gyokuro its distinctive savory, almost brothy character.

faq.question: How should gyokuro be brewed differently from sencha?
faq.answer: Gyokuro is brewed at a much lower temperature, around 50 to 60 degrees Celsius, compared to sencha's 70 to 80 degrees. Use more leaf and less water, steeping for two minutes. This gentle extraction highlights the sweetness and umami without pulling out bitter compounds.
